value.overview: The Slaty Finch is a small, secretive tanager of humid mountain forests and bamboo-rich clearings in Central America and the northern Andes. Males are mostly slate gray, while females and young birds are browner and less distinctive. It is usually uncommon and local, but numbers can increase sharply where native bamboo produces seeds. In Costa Rica, it is an uncommon highland bird associated mainly with the country’s major mountain ranges.
value.classification: The Slaty Finch belongs to the tanager family Thraupidae and the order Passeriformes. It is commonly listed as Haplospiza rustica, although the currently recognized genus in some modern classifications is Spodiornis, giving the name Spodiornis rusticus.
value.identification: This small finch is about 12–13 cm long and has a short, pointed, conical bill. Adult males are largely uniform lead-gray or slate-gray, with darker wings and tail. Females are mainly dark olive-brown to brown, and immature birds are grayish with brown feather edges and some brownish coloring below. The species can be difficult to detect in dense vegetation. Its plain plumage, compact shape, and association with high-elevation bamboo help distinguish it from other mountain finches.
value.rangeHabitat: The Slaty Finch occurs from southern Mexico through Central America and in the northern Andes of South America. In Costa Rica it is a rare or very local resident, with records from the principal mountain chains, although it has not been reliably reported from the Cordillera de Guanacaste. It occurs above about 1,500 m in the Cordillera de Tilarán and generally from 1,850 m upward in the Central Volcanic and Talamanca ranges, reaching the upper limit of tree growth. Habitats include humid montane forest, forest edges, second growth, clearings, and bamboo stands.
value.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the species is considered resident but may make irregular, seasonal, possibly nomadic movements. These movements appear to be linked partly to the availability and seeding of native bamboo rather than to regular long-distance migration.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited, but nesting has been documented in the highlands of Costa Rica. A studied nest was an elongated, globular structure placed about 3 m above the ground in a fork of a moss- and epiphyte-covered tree. The nest contained four dull-white eggs. Breeding activity and local abundance may increase when Chusquea bamboo is producing seed. Males sing from perches in forest understory and second-growth vegetation during the breeding period.
value.dietFeeding: The Slaty Finch is primarily a seed-eater, with native bamboo seeds probably forming an important seasonal food source. It forages in understory vegetation, forest edges, clearings, and bamboo patches, often where dense seed crops are available. Its short, pointed bill is suited to handling seeds. Direct information on the relative importance of insects, fruit, and other plant foods is limited.
value.behavior: This species is generally quiet and inconspicuous in dense mountain vegetation. It often travels in small flocks and may gather in larger numbers around fruiting or seeding bamboo. Singing males use elevated perches within forest or second growth, but the species is more often detected by brief movements and calls than by prolonged views. Its abundance can fluctuate locally as bamboo flowering and seeding events change the available food supply.

conservation.populationTrend: Population trend is not well documented; the global trend is best treated as unknown.
